title: Limit definition of the derivative

symbols.y': the derivative of y with respect to x, i.e. the slope of the curve at a point
symbols.\\Delta x: a small change in the input variable x
symbols.\\Delta y: the change in the output y caused by that change in x

explanation: Refer to the Differential Calculus section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. The derivative is the limiting value of the ratio of output change to input change as the input change shrinks to zero.
example:
Find the derivative of \(f(x) = x^2\) at \(x = 3\) using the limit definition.

$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0}\frac{(x + \Delta x)^2 - x^2}{\Delta x}$$

$$= \lim_{\Delta x \to 0}\frac{2x\,\Delta x + (\Delta x)^2}{\Delta x}$$

$$= \lim_{\Delta x \to 0}\left(2x + \Delta x\right)$$

$$= 2x = 2(3) = 6$$

title: Partial derivative notation
equation: \(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\ \text{for}\ z = f(x, y)\ \text{with } y \text{ held fixed}\)

symbols.z: the dependent variable, a function z = f(x, y) of two independent variables
symbols.\\partial z / \\partial x: the partial derivative of z with respect to x, found by treating y as a constant

explanation: Refer to The Partial Derivative section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. When one variable is held fixed, the two-variable function behaves like a single-variable function in the remaining variable.
example:
Find \(\partial z/\partial x\) for \(z = 3x^2y + xy^2\), then evaluate at \(x = 2,\ y = 1\).

$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(3x^2y + xy^2\right)$$

$$= 3y \cdot 2x + y^2 = 6xy + y^2$$

Substituting \(x = 2\) and \(y = 1\):

$$= 6(2)(1) + (1)^2$$

$$= 12 + 1 = 13$$

title: Definite integral as a limit of Riemann sums

symbols.n: the number of subintervals the interval [a, b] is divided into
symbols.x_i: a sample point in the i-th subinterval
symbols.\\Delta x_i: the width of the i-th subinterval, which goes to zero for every i as n grows

explanation: Refer to the Integral Calculus section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. The definite integral is the limit, as the subintervals shrink, of the sum of rectangle areas under the curve.
example:
Estimate \(\int_0^2 x\,dx\) with a right-endpoint Riemann sum using \(n = 4\) subintervals.

$$\Delta x = \frac{2 - 0}{4} = 0.5$$

$$\sum_{i=1}^{4} f(x_i)\,\Delta x = 0.5\,(0.5 + 1.0 + 1.5 + 2.0)$$

$$= 0.5\,(5.0) = 2.5$$

The exact integral is \(x^2/2\big|_0^2 = 2\), so the estimate 2.5 approaches the true value as \(n\) grows.

title: Solution of first-order linear homogeneous ODE

symbols.y': the derivative of the unknown function y with respect to its variable
symbols.C: a constant fixed by the initial condition
symbols.t: the independent variable (time in transient problems)

explanation: Refer to the Differential Equations section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. A first-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients has an exponential solution that decays (or grows) at rate a.
example:
Solve \(y' + 3y = 0\) with \(y(0) = 5\), then evaluate at \(t = 1\).

$$y(t) = Ce^{-3t}$$

Apply the initial condition \(y(0) = 5\):

$$5 = Ce^{0} \;\Longrightarrow\; C = 5$$

$$y(t) = 5e^{-3t}$$

At \(t = 1\):

$$y(1) = 5e^{-3}$$

$$\approx 5(0.0498) = 0.249$$

title: Matrix inverse from the adjoint

symbols.A^{-1}: the inverse of the square matrix A; satisfies A A^{-1} = A^{-1} A = I
symbols.\\text{adj}(A): the adjoint of A, formed by replacing the elements of the transpose with their cofactors
symbols.|A|: the determinant of A; the inverse exists only when this is nonzero

explanation: Refer to the Matrices section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. A square matrix can be inverted by dividing its adjoint by its determinant.
example:
Invert \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

$$|A| = (2)(1) - (1)(1)$$

$$= 1$$

$$\text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$$

$$A^{-1} = \frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$$

Check: \(A A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = I\).

title: Second-order determinant
equation: \(\begin{vmatrix} a_1 & a_2 \\ b_1 & b_2 \end{vmatrix} = a_1b_2 - a_2b_1\)

symbols.a_1, a_2: the elements of the first row of the determinant
symbols.b_1, b_2: the elements of the second row of the determinant

explanation: Refer to the Determinants section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. A two-by-two determinant is the product of the main diagonal minus the product of the off diagonal.

title: Dot product of two vectors

symbols.a_x, a_y, a_z: the scalar components of vector A along the i, j, k axes
symbols.b_x, b_y, b_z: the scalar components of vector B along the i, j, k axes
symbols.A, B: the magnitudes (lengths) of vectors A and B
symbols.\\theta: the angle between the two vectors

explanation: Refer to the Vectors section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. The dot product is a scalar equal to the projection of one vector onto the other times its length; it is zero when the vectors are perpendicular.
example:
Find \(\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{B}\) for \(\mathbf{A} = 2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j} - \mathbf{k}\) and \(\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + 4\mathbf{k}\).

$$\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{B} = (2)(1) + (3)(-2) + (-1)(4)$$

$$= 2 - 6 - 4$$

$$= -8$$

title: Multiplication of complex numbers in polar form

symbols.z_1, z_2: complex numbers written in polar form, z = c(cos θ + j sin θ) = c∠θ
symbols.c_1, c_2: the magnitudes (moduli) of z_1 and z_2
symbols.\\theta_1, \\theta_2: the angles (arguments) of z_1 and z_2

explanation: Refer to the Algebra of Complex Numbers section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. In polar form, multiplying two complex numbers multiplies their magnitudes and adds their angles.
example:
Multiply \(z_1 = 4\angle 30^\circ\) by \(z_2 = 2\angle 15^\circ\).

$$z_1 z_2 = (4 \times 2)\,\angle\,(30^\circ + 15^\circ)$$

$$= 8\,\angle\,45^\circ$$

title: Law of total probability

symbols.P(A + B): the probability that event A occurs, or event B occurs, or both occur
symbols.P(A), P(B): the individual probabilities that A and B occur
symbols.P(A, B): the joint probability that A and B occur simultaneously

explanation: Refer to the Laws of Probability section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. Adding the two individual probabilities double-counts the overlap, so the joint probability is subtracted once.

section: Dispersion, Mean, Median, and Mode Values
title: Sample variance

symbols.s^2: the sample variance, measuring the spread of the sampled data
symbols.n: the number of observations in the sample
symbols.X_i: the value of the i-th observation
symbols.\\bar{X}: the arithmetic mean of the sample

explanation: Refer to the Dispersion, Mean, Median, and Mode Values section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. The sample variance averages the squared deviations from the mean, dividing by n − 1 rather than n.

title: Normal probability density function

symbols.f(x): the density of the normal distribution at the value x
symbols.\\mu: the population mean; the center (mode) of the symmetric curve
symbols.\\sigma: the population standard deviation; controls the width of the curve
symbols.x: any real value, with the curve inflecting one standard deviation on either side of the mean

explanation: Refer to the Normal Distribution (Gaussian Distribution) section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. The bell-shaped density is centered at the mean, and its spread is set entirely by the standard deviation.
example:
Evaluate the normal density at its center for \(\mu = 100\) and \(\sigma = 15\).

$$f(100) = \frac{1}{15\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{100-100}{15}\right)^2}$$

$$= \frac{1}{15\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{0}$$

$$= \frac{1}{15(2.5066)}$$

$$\approx 0.0266$$

title: Binomial probability of x successes

symbols.P_n(x): the probability of exactly x successes in n independent trials
symbols.x: the number of successes, from 0 to n
symbols.p: the probability of success on a single trial
symbols.q: the probability of failure on a single trial, q = 1 − p
symbols.C(n,x): the number of combinations of n items taken x at a time

explanation: Refer to the Binomial Distribution section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. Each specific sequence of x successes has probability p^x q^(n−x), and there are C(n, x) such sequences.
example:
Find the probability of exactly 2 successes in 10 trials with \(p = 0.3\).

$$P_{10}(2) = \frac{10!}{2!\,8!}\,(0.3)^2(0.7)^8$$

$$= 45\,(0.09)(0.05765)$$

$$\approx 0.2335$$

section: Confidence Intervals, Sample Distributions and Sample Size
title: Two-sided confidence interval for the mean

symbols.\\bar{x}: the sample mean, the center of the interval
symbols.z_{\\alpha/2}: the standard normal value cutting off probability α/2 in the upper tail for the chosen confidence level
symbols.\\alpha: one minus the confidence level (e.g. 0.05 for a 95% interval)

explanation: Refer to the Confidence Intervals, Sample Distributions and Sample Size section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. Note: in FE Reference Handbook 10.6 the interval for the mean is displayed in a figure in this section (printed p. 75); the plain-text extraction of the handbook does not reproduce the figure's formula. The interval centers on the sample mean and widens with more variability and shrinks with more data.

section: Probability and Density Functions: Means and Variances
title: Poisson distribution: mass function, mean, variance

symbols.f(x;\\lambda): the probability of exactly x events occurring
symbols.\\lambda: the average number of events in the interval; it equals both the mean and the variance

explanation: Refer to the Probability and Density Functions: Means and Variances section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. The Poisson model counts events in a fixed interval, and its mean and variance are the same number.
example:
A call center averages 3 calls per minute. Find the probability of exactly 2 calls in a minute.

$$f(2; 3) = \frac{3^2 e^{-3}}{2!}$$

$$= \frac{9(0.0498)}{2}$$

$$\approx 0.224$$

The mean and variance are both \(\lambda = 3\).

title: Expected value of a discrete random variable

symbols.E[X]: the expected (average) value of the random variable X
symbols.x_k: the k-th possible value of X
symbols.f(x_k): the probability mass at x_k, i.e. the probability that X equals x_k

explanation: Refer to the Expected Values section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. The expected value is a probability-weighted average of all possible outcomes.

section: Linear Regression and Goodness of Fit
title: Least-squares regression slope

symbols.\\hat{b}: the estimated slope of the fitted line ŷ = â + b̂x
symbols.\\hat{a}: the estimated y-intercept of the fitted line
symbols.S_{xy}: the sum of products of x- and y-deviations from their means, S_xy = Σx_i y_i − (Σx_i)(Σy_i)/n
symbols.S_{xx}: the sum of squared x-deviations from the mean, S_xx = Σx_i² − (Σx_i)²/n
symbols.\\bar{x}, \\bar{y}: the sample means of the x and y data

explanation: Refer to the Linear Regression and Goodness of Fit section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. The least-squares line minimizes the total squared vertical miss, which forces the slope to be the ratio of S_xy to S_xx.

title: Sinking fund factor

symbols.(A/F, i\\%, n): the factor converting a future amount F into an equivalent uniform series A
symbols.F: the future amount accumulated after n periods

explanation: Refer to the Uniform Series section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. The sinking fund factor gives the equal periodic deposit that will grow to a target future sum.

title: Uniform series present worth factor

symbols.(P/A, i\\%, n): the factor converting a uniform series A into an equivalent present worth P
symbols.P: the present worth (value today) of the series

explanation: Refer to the Uniform Series section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. The present worth factor collapses a stream of equal payments into a single equivalent value today.

title: Straight-line depreciation

symbols.D_j: the depreciation charge in year j (the same every year under straight line)
symbols.C: the initial cost of the asset
symbols.S_n: the expected salvage value at the end of the asset's life
symbols.n: the depreciable life of the asset in years

explanation: Refer to the Depreciation section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. Straight-line depreciation spreads the loss of value (cost minus salvage) evenly over the asset's life.
example:
An asset costs \(C = \$50{,}000\), has salvage \(S_n = \$5{,}000\), and a 9-year life. Find the annual depreciation.

$$D_j = \frac{50{,}000 - 5{,}000}{9}$$

$$= \frac{45{,}000}{9}$$

$$= \$5{,}000\ \text{per year}$$

title: Capitalized cost of a perpetual series

symbols.P: the capitalized cost, i.e. the present worth of a perpetual uniform series
symbols.A: the uniform amount paid every period, forever

explanation: Refer to the Capitalized Costs section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. A payment that repeats forever is worth today the annual amount divided by the interest rate.
example:
What lump sum today funds \(A = \$1{,}200\) per year forever at \(i = 6\%\)?

$$P = \frac{1{,}200}{0.06}$$

$$= \$20{,}000$$

title: Rate-of-return (IRR) condition

symbols.ROR: the rate-of-return (internal rate of return) on the investment
symbols.PW(\\text{benefits}): the present worth of all benefit cash flows, discounted at the rate-of-return
symbols.PW(\\text{costs}): the present worth of all cost cash flows, discounted at the rate-of-return
symbols.i: the interest rate that makes the two present worths equal

explanation: Refer to the Rate-of-Return section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. Note: the rate-of-return equation is not printed in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6; the section (printed p. 235) states only in words that the rate-of-return is the interest rate that makes the benefits and costs equal. The project is acceptable when its rate-of-return exceeds the minimum acceptable rate (MARR).
example:
A project costs \$10,000 now and returns \$2,500 per year for 5 years. Find the rate-of-return.

$$2{,}500\,(P/A, i\%, 5) = 10{,}000$$

$$(P/A, i\%, 5) = 4.0000$$

From interest tables, \((P/A, 7\%, 5) = 4.1002\) and \((P/A, 8\%, 5) = 3.9927\), so:

$$i \approx 7.93\%$$

title: Benefit-cost ratio decision rule

symbols.B: the present worth (or equivalent uniform value) of the project's benefits
symbols.C: the present worth (or equivalent uniform value) of the project's costs

explanation: Refer to the Benefit-Cost Analysis section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. A project is justified when its benefits at least cover its costs, i.e. the ratio of benefits to costs is one or more.
example:
A project has benefits \(B = \$180{,}000\) and costs \(C = \$150{,}000\) (same worth basis). Is it acceptable?

$$B/C = \frac{180{,}000}{150{,}000}$$

$$= 1.2$$

Since \(1.2 \ge 1\), the project is acceptable.

title: Force and moment equilibrium

symbols.F_n: each individual force acting on the body
symbols.M_n: each individual moment acting on the body, taken about any single point

explanation: A body stays at rest only when every force on it cancels out and every twisting effect cancels out as well. On the exam these two vector sums expand into the scalar equations you solve for unknown reactions.
example:
A 200-N sign hangs from two symmetric cables, each at 30 deg above the horizontal.
Let T = tension in each cable. Vertical forces must sum to zero:
\(2T\sin(30^\circ) - 200 = 0\)
\(T = \dfrac{200}{2\sin(30^\circ)}\)
\(T = \dfrac{200}{1} = 200\ \text{N}\)

title: Resultant force and moment of a force system

symbols.F: single force equivalent to the entire system
symbols.M: single moment equivalent to the entire system about the reference point
symbols.F_n: one force belonging to the system
symbols.r_n: position vector from the reference point to the line of action of F_n

explanation: Any collection of forces can be traded for one net push plus one net twist about a chosen point. Picking the point cleverly, for example at an unknown reaction, makes the moment equation much shorter.
example:
A 50-N force pushes straight down at a point 3 m to the right of point O.
The equivalent moment about O is:
\(M_O = r \times F\)
\(M_O = (3\ \text{m})(50\ \text{N})\)
\(M_O = 150\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}\) clockwise

title: Joint equilibrium equations

symbols.F_H: horizontal force or horizontal component of a member force at the joint
symbols.F_V: vertical force or vertical component of a member force at the joint

explanation: Cut the truss joint by joint and treat each pin as a particle in equilibrium. Two equations per joint means you can solve for two unknown member forces at a time, so start at a joint with only two unknowns.
example:
At a truss joint a 10-kN load pulls straight down.
Two members leave the joint symmetrically at 45 deg above the horizontal.
Vertical equilibrium at the joint:
\(2F\sin(45^\circ) - 10 = 0\)
\(F = \dfrac{10}{2\sin(45^\circ)}\)
\(F = \dfrac{10}{1.414} = 7.07\ \text{kN}\) (tension)

section: Centroids of Masses, Areas, Lengths, and Volumes
title: Centroid of discrete masses and composite areas
equation: \(r_c = \dfrac{\sum m_n r_n}{\sum m_n}, \quad x_{ac} = \dfrac{\sum x_n a_n}{A}\)

symbols.r_c: position vector of the centroid (center of mass) of the system
symbols.r_n: position vector of particle n from the reference point
symbols.x_ac: x-coordinate of the centroid of a composite area
symbols.x_n: x-coordinate of the centroid of sub-area n
symbols.A: total area, the sum of all sub-areas

explanation: The centroid is the weighted-average position of whatever you are averaging: mass, area, length, or volume. Split a composite shape into simple rectangles and triangles, then average their individual centroids weighted by size.
example:
Two point masses: 2 kg at x = 0 m and 6 kg at x = 4 m.
Center of mass:
\(x_c = \dfrac{m_1 x_1 + m_2 x_2}{m_1 + m_2}\)
\(x_c = \dfrac{(2)(0) + (6)(4)}{2 + 6}\)
\(x_c = \dfrac{24}{8} = 3\ \text{m}\)

title: Two-force body equilibrium

symbols.F_1: the first of the two forces acting on the body
symbols.F_2: the second of the two forces acting on the body

explanation: When every force's line of action passes through one point, the system can only balance if the forces add to zero there. The classic case is a body with just two forces: they must be equal in size, opposite in direction, and share one line of action.
example:
A strut pinned at both ends receives a 500-N push at one pin.
For equilibrium the other pin must push back equally, oppositely, and collinearly:
\(F_1 + F_2 = 0\)
\(F_2 = -F_1 = -500\ \text{N}\)
The strut carries 500 N in pure compression.

title: Limiting static friction

symbols.F: friction force resisting the impending sliding motion
symbols.mu_s: coefficient of static friction between the two contacting surfaces
symbols.N: normal force pressing the two surfaces together

explanation: Static friction only pushes back as hard as it must, up to a ceiling set by the surfaces. If the force trying to slide the object exceeds mu_s times N, the contact breaks loose and motion starts.
example:
A 100-N crate rests on a floor with mu_s = 0.4.
Normal force: N = 100 N.
Largest friction the contact can supply:
\(F_{max} = \mu_s N\)
\(F_{max} = (0.4)(100)\)
\(F_{max} = 40\ \text{N}\)
A 30-N push will not move the crate; a 50-N push will.

title: Magnitude and direction of a planar resultant

symbols.F: magnitude of the single resultant force
symbols.theta: direction angle of the resultant measured from the positive x-axis

explanation: Add all the x-pieces together and all the y-pieces together, then rebuild one arrow from those two sums. The arctangent gives the arrow's direction, so watch the component signs to land in the correct quadrant.
example:
Forces on a bracket: 30 N to the right and 40 N upward.
Component sums: sum F_x = 30 N, sum F_y = 40 N.
Resultant magnitude:
\(F = \sqrt{30^2 + 40^2}\)
\(F = \sqrt{2500} = 50\ \text{N}\)
Direction:
\(\theta = \arctan(40/30) = 53.1^\circ\) above the x-axis.

title: Conservation of mechanical energy with nonconservative work

symbols.T_1: kinetic energy of the particle at state 1
symbols.T_2: kinetic energy of the particle at state 2
symbols.V_1: potential energy of the particle at state 1
symbols.V_2: potential energy of the particle at state 2
symbols.U_{1->2}: work done by nonconservative forces (such as friction) moving between states 1 and 2

explanation: Energy at the finish equals energy at the start, plus whatever nonconservative forces added or drained along the way. It is the go-to tool when a problem gives positions and speeds but no time information.
example:
A 2-kg block slides from rest down a frictionless 5-m-high ramp.
T_1 = 0, V_1 = mgh, V_2 = 0, and no nonconservative work:
\(\tfrac{1}{2} m v_2^2 = mgh\)
\(v_2 = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2(9.81)(5)}\)
\(v_2 = 9.90\ \text{m/s}\)

title: Newton's second law for a particle

symbols.sum F: vector sum of all forces acting on the particle

explanation: Add the forces as vectors and the result must equal mass times acceleration. Draw the free-body diagram first, because this equation is only as good as the forces you remember to include.
example:
A 5-kg block is pulled by a 20-N horizontal force on a frictionless surface.
Newton's second law along the motion:
\(\sum F = ma\)
\(20 = (5)a\)
\(a = 4\ \text{m/s}^2\)

title: Velocity and acceleration as time derivatives

symbols.v: instantaneous velocity vector of the particle
symbols.r: position vector of the particle in an inertial frame
symbols.a: instantaneous acceleration vector of the particle

explanation: Velocity is the rate at which position changes, and acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes. Differentiate to travel from position toward acceleration; integrate, carrying the starting values along, to go the other way.
example:
A particle moves in one dimension with position r(t) = 3t^2 meters.
Velocity is the time derivative of position:
\(v = \dfrac{dr}{dt} = 6t\)
At t = 2 s:
\(v = 6(2) = 12\ \text{m/s}\)

title: Linear impulse-momentum for a particle

symbols.F: net force vector acting on the particle
symbols.integral: linear impulse: the total push delivered by F over the time interval

explanation: Momentum at the end equals momentum at the start plus the total push delivered over the elapsed time. Reach for it when a force acts over a known time, as in collisions, kicks, and impacts.
example:
A 0.5-kg ball moving at 10 m/s is brought to rest in 0.05 s.
Impulse-momentum along the motion:
\(m v_2 - m v_1 = F_{avg}\,\Delta t\)
\(0 - (0.5)(10) = F_{avg}(0.05)\)
\(F_{avg} = \dfrac{-5}{0.05} = -100\ \text{N}\)
The average stopping force is 100 N opposite the motion.

title: Tangential and normal acceleration components

symbols.a_t: tangential acceleration: the part that changes the speed
symbols.a_n: normal acceleration: the part that changes the direction of motion
symbols.v: speed of the particle along its path
symbols.rho: radius of curvature of the path at the particle's location

explanation: On a curved path acceleration splits into two jobs: one changes how fast you go, the other bends your heading toward the inside of the curve. The normal part is always speed squared over the local radius.
example:
A car rounds a 50-m-radius curve at a constant 20 m/s.
Speed is constant, so a_t = 0.
Normal acceleration:
\(a_n = \dfrac{v^2}{\rho}\)
\(a_n = \dfrac{20^2}{50} = \dfrac{400}{50}\)
\(a_n = 8\ \text{m/s}^2\) toward the center of the curve.

section: Rigid Body Rotation About a Fixed Axis
title: Torque equals spin inertia times angular acceleration

symbols.sum T: sum of the torques about the fixed axis of rotation
symbols.I: mass moment of inertia about the axis of rotation
symbols.alpha: angular acceleration about the axis of rotation

explanation: This is the rotational twin of F = ma: net torque about the fixed axle equals the body's spin inertia times its angular acceleration. Mass sitting farther from the axle counts more, which is exactly what I captures.
example:
A 12-N·m torque is applied to a wheel with I = 3 kg·m² about its axle.
Rotational equation of motion:
\(\sum T = I\alpha\)
\(12 = (3)\alpha\)
\(\alpha = 4\ \text{rad/s}^2\)

title: Equation of motion of a damped spring-mass system

symbols.x: displacement measured from the equilibrium position (dots denote time derivatives)
symbols.F: externally applied force; zero for free vibration

explanation: One equation tells the whole mass-spring-damper story: inertia resists speeding up, the damper bleeds motion away, and the spring pulls back toward center. Set F to zero for free vibration; make F periodic for forced vibration.
example:
A 4-kg mass hangs from a spring with k = 100 N/m, no damping, no forcing.
Equation of motion:
\(4\ddot{x} + 100x = 0\)
Divide by 4: x-double-dot + 25x = 0, so the natural frequency is:
\(\omega_n = \sqrt{25} = 5\ \text{rad/s}\)

title: Position, velocity, and acceleration of A relative to B
equation: \(r_A = r_B + r_{A/B}, \quad v_A = v_B + v_{A/B}, \quad a_A = a_B + a_{A/B}\)

symbols.r_{A/B}: position of A measured relative to B (and likewise for v and a)

explanation: What A does equals what B does plus what A does as seen from B. It is careful bookkeeping for moving reference points, like finding a walker's ground speed on a moving train.
example:
A train B moves at 25 m/s while passenger A walks forward at 2 m/s relative to the train.
Absolute velocity of the passenger:
\(v_A = v_B + v_{A/B}\)
\(v_A = 25 + 2\)
\(v_A = 27\ \text{m/s}\) relative to the ground.

title: Axial stress and elastic elongation

symbols.sigma: axial stress on the cross section
symbols.delta: elastic change in length of the member
symbols.E: modulus of elasticity of the material

explanation: Pull a bar and two things happen: the stress is simply force over area, and the stretch grows with load and length but shrinks with a fatter section or stiffer material. Both formulas assume the stress stays below yielding.
example:
Steel bar: P = 20,000 N, A = 400 mm², L = 2 m, E = 200 GPa.
Axial stress:
\(\sigma = \dfrac{P}{A}\)
\(\sigma = \dfrac{20{,}000}{400 \times 10^{-6}} = 50 \times 10^6\ \text{Pa} = 50\ \text{MPa}\)
Elongation:
\(\delta = \dfrac{PL}{AE}\)
\(\delta = \dfrac{(20{,}000)(2)}{(400 \times 10^{-6})(200 \times 10^9)}\)
\(\delta = 5.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m} = 0.5\ \text{mm}\)

title: Euler critical buckling load

symbols.P_cr: critical axial load at which the column begins to buckle
symbols.I: smallest area moment of inertia of the cross section
symbols.K: effective-length factor accounting for the end supports

explanation: A long slender column fails by bowing sideways long before the material itself yields, and Euler's formula gives the load where that bowing starts. Shortening the effective length pays off fast because length is squared in the denominator.
example:
Pinned-pinned steel column: L = 3 m, K = 1.0, EI = 50,000 N·m².
Critical buckling load:
\(P_{cr} = \dfrac{\pi^2 EI}{(KL)^2}\)
\(P_{cr} = \dfrac{\pi^2 (50{,}000)}{(1.0 \times 3)^2}\)
\(P_{cr} = \dfrac{493{,}480}{9} = 54{,}831\ \text{N} \approx 54.8\ \text{kN}\)

title: Bending normal stress

symbols.sigma_x: normal stress from bending at the fiber
symbols.M: bending moment at the cross section
symbols.y: distance of the fiber from the neutral axis
symbols.I: area moment of inertia of the cross section about the neutral axis

explanation: Bending stress is zero at the neutral axis and grows linearly to a maximum at the outermost fibers, tension on one side and compression on the other. The sign keeps track of which side is which for the chosen coordinates.
example:
Beam with M = 10 kN·m, I = 8×10⁻⁶ m⁴, outer fiber at y = 0.1 m.
Bending stress at the outer fiber:
\(\sigma_x = -\dfrac{My}{I}\)
\(\sigma_x = -\dfrac{(10{,}000)(0.1)}{8 \times 10^{-6}}\)
\(\sigma_x = -125 \times 10^6\ \text{Pa} = -125\ \text{MPa}\)

title: Differential equation of the deflection curve

symbols.I: area moment of inertia of the cross section
symbols.M: bending moment, as a function of x

explanation: The bending moment is proportional to the beam's curvature, which yields a differential equation for the bent shape. Integrate twice and use the supports, zero deflection at a pin and zero slope at a wall, to fix the integration constants.
example:
Cantilever beam: tip load P = 1,000 N, L = 2 m, EI = 40,000 N·m².
Double integration with y(0) = 0 and y'(0) = 0 gives the tip deflection:
\(y_{tip} = -\dfrac{PL^3}{3EI}\)
\(y_{tip} = -\dfrac{(1{,}000)(2)^3}{3(40{,}000)}\)
\(y_{tip} = -\dfrac{8{,}000}{120{,}000} = -0.0667\ \text{m} = -66.7\ \text{mm}\)

title: Torsional shear stress and angle of twist

symbols.tau: shear stress from torsion at radius r
symbols.r: radial distance from the shaft center
symbols.J: polar moment of inertia of the cross section
symbols.phi: total angle of twist, in radians

explanation: Twisting stress is zero at the shaft's center and largest at the outer surface, growing in direct proportion to radius. The total twist angle grows with torque and length, and shrinks with stiffer material and a stockier cross section.
example:
Solid shaft: T = 500 N·m, outer radius r = 0.025 m, J = 6.14×10⁻⁷ m⁴.
Maximum shear stress at the surface:
\(\tau = \dfrac{Tr}{J}\)
\(\tau = \dfrac{(500)(0.025)}{6.14 \times 10^{-7}}\)
\(\tau = 20.4 \times 10^6\ \text{Pa} = 20.4\ \text{MPa}\)

title: Free thermal expansion of a bar

symbols.delta_t: change in length caused by the temperature change
symbols.alpha: temperature coefficient of expansion of the material

explanation: Heat a free bar and it grows in proportion to its length and the temperature swing; cool it and it shrinks the same way. If something blocks that growth, the trapped deformation turns into thermal stress instead.
example:
Steel rod: L = 5 m, alpha = 12×10⁻⁶/°C, heated from 20 °C to 70 °C.
Thermal elongation:
\(\delta_t = \alpha L\,(T - T_0)\)
\(\delta_t = (12 \times 10^{-6})(5)(70 - 20)\)
\(\delta_t = 3.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m} = 3.0\ \text{mm}\)

title: In-plane principal stresses (2D stress state)

symbols.sigma_a: one in-plane principal stress (the larger becomes sigma_1 after ordering)
symbols.sigma_b: the other in-plane principal stress (the smaller becomes sigma_3 after ordering)
symbols.sigma_x: normal stress acting on the x-face of the element
symbols.sigma_y: normal stress acting on the y-face of the element
symbols.tau_xy: shear stress acting on the element

explanation: At every point there is an orientation where the shear stress vanishes and the normal stresses reach their extremes; those are the principal stresses. This formula finds them directly from the stresses on the x- and y-faces, no rotation needed.
example:
Stress element: sigma_x = 80 MPa, sigma_y = -20 MPa, tau_xy = 30 MPa.
Average normal stress:
\(\dfrac{80 + (-20)}{2} = 30\ \text{MPa}\)
Radius term:
\(R = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{80 - (-20)}{2}\right)^2 + 30^2} = \sqrt{50^2 + 30^2}\)
\(R = \sqrt{3400} = 58.3\ \text{MPa}\)
\(\sigma_a = 30 + 58.3 = 88.3\ \text{MPa}, \quad \sigma_b = 30 - 58.3 = -28.3\ \text{MPa}\)

title: Thin-wall hoop and axial stress

symbols.sigma_t: hoop (tangential) stress in the cylinder wall
symbols.sigma_a: axial stress in the cylinder wall
symbols.t: wall thickness (thin-wall approximation applies when t is about one-tenth of the inside radius or less)

explanation: Internal pressure tries to split a thin cylinder two ways: around its circumference and along its length. The hoop direction carries the bigger load, exactly twice the axial stress.
example:
Thin tank: P = 2 MPa, r = 0.5 m, t = 0.01 m (t = r/50, so thin-wall applies).
Hoop stress:
\(\sigma_t = \dfrac{Pr}{t}\)
\(\sigma_t = \dfrac{(2)(0.5)}{0.01} = 100\ \text{MPa}\)
Axial stress:
\(\sigma_a = \dfrac{Pr}{2t} = 50\ \text{MPa}\)

title: Electrical resistivity of a conductor
explanation: Resistivity is the material's own opposition to current with shape factored out: resistance grows with length and shrinks with area, and rho is the constant that makes that true. Conductivity is simply its reciprocal.
example:
Copper wire: R = 0.5 ohm, L = 100 m, A = 3.31 mm².
Resistivity:
\(\rho = \dfrac{RA}{L}\)
\(\rho = \dfrac{(0.5)(3.31 \times 10^{-6})}{100}\)
\(\rho = 1.66 \times 10^{-8}\ \Omega\cdot\text{m}\)

title: Bernoulli energy balance between two sections

symbols.z_1: elevation of section 1 above a datum
symbols.z_2: elevation of section 2 above a datum

explanation: With no friction and no pump between two points, pressure head plus velocity head plus elevation head stays constant; energy just trades among the three forms. It is the energy equation with the loss term set to zero.
example:
Horizontal pipe: P_1 = 200 kPa, v_1 = 2 m/s, v_2 = 4 m/s, water gamma = 9.79 kN/m³, z_1 = z_2.
Bernoulli between the sections:
\(\dfrac{P_1}{\gamma} + \dfrac{v_1^2}{2g} = \dfrac{P_2}{\gamma} + \dfrac{v_2^2}{2g}\)
\(\dfrac{200}{9.79} + \dfrac{2^2}{2(9.81)} = \dfrac{P_2}{9.79} + \dfrac{4^2}{2(9.81)}\)
\(20.43 + 0.204 = \dfrac{P_2}{9.79} + 0.815\)
\(P_2 = 9.79 \times 19.82 = 194\ \text{kPa}\)

title: Pressure drop for a fluid of constant density

symbols.h_f: head loss from friction between the two sections

explanation: When a pipe keeps the same diameter and elevation, velocity and height cancel out of the energy equation, leaving the pressure drop equal to the friction loss converted back into pressure. A denser fluid loses more pressure for the same head loss.
example:
Water (gamma = 9.79 kN/m³) flows through a constant-diameter horizontal pipe with h_f = 3 m.
Pressure drop:
\(P_1 - P_2 = \gamma\,h_f\)
\(P_1 - P_2 = (9.79)(3)\)
\(P_1 - P_2 = 29.4\ \text{kPa}\)

section: The Pressure Field in a Static Liquid
title: Hydrostatic pressure difference between two points

symbols.h: vertical distance between the two points

explanation: In a still liquid, pressure depends only on depth: go deeper and it rises by the specific weight times the depth. The minus sign is the bookkeeping that says higher elevation means lower pressure.
example:
Find the gauge pressure 4 m below the surface of water (gamma = 9.79 kN/m³); surface pressure is atmospheric, so gauge is zero there.
With depth h measured downward, P = gamma·h:
\(P = (9.79)(4)\)
\(P = 39.2\ \text{kPa gauge}\)

title: Buoyant force equals weight of displaced fluid

symbols.F_b: buoyant force pushing upward on the body
symbols.V_displaced: volume of fluid pushed aside by the submerged portion of the body

explanation: A submerged or floating body is pushed up with a force equal to the weight of the fluid it shoves out of the way. A floating body settles at exactly the depth where that upward push matches its own weight.
example:
A 0.5-m³ block floats in water (gamma = 9.79 kN/m³) with 60% of its volume submerged.
Displaced volume:
\(V_{displaced} = (0.60)(0.5) = 0.3\ \text{m}^3\)
Buoyant force:
\(F_b = \gamma\,V_{displaced}\)
\(F_b = (9.79)(0.3) = 2.94\ \text{kN}\)
The block therefore weighs 2.94 kN.

title: Volume and mass flow rate for one-dimensional flow
explanation: What flows in must flow out: for steady flow the mass rate is identical at every cross section. If the fluid is incompressible as well, the volume rate Q is constant too, so narrowing the pipe forces the fluid to speed up.
example:
Water flows at 3 m/s through a pipe of diameter 0.1 m.
Flow area:
\(A = \dfrac{\pi d^2}{4} = \dfrac{\pi(0.1)^2}{4}\)
\(A = 0.007854\ \text{m}^2\)
Volume flow rate:
\(Q = A\,v = (0.007854)(3)\)
\(Q = 0.0236\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}\)

title: Simple manometer pressure relation

symbols.P_2: known reference pressure at the other end
symbols.gamma_1: specific weight of the first manometer fluid
symbols.gamma_2: specific weight of the second manometer fluid
symbols.h_1: column height of the first fluid
symbols.h_2: column height of the second fluid

explanation: A manometer reads pressure by balancing it against fluid columns: walk from the unknown pressure to the known one, adding gamma·h when moving down a column and subtracting it when moving up. Different fluids simply contribute different gammas.
example:
U-tube open to the atmosphere (P_2 = 0 gauge), mercury column h_2 = 0.2 m (gamma_2 = 133.1 kN/m³), water column h_1 = 0.1 m (gamma_1 = 9.79 kN/m³).
Manometer equation:
\(P_0 = P_2 + \gamma_2 h_2 - \gamma_1 h_1\)
\(P_0 = 0 + (133.1)(0.2) - (9.79)(0.1)\)
\(P_0 = 26.62 - 0.979 = 25.6\ \text{kPa gauge}\)

title: Power required to pump a fluid through a head

symbols.W_dot: power that the pump and motor together must draw
symbols.h: head the fluid must be lifted
symbols.eta_t: total efficiency, pump efficiency times motor efficiency

explanation: Pump power is the weight of fluid moved per second times how high it must go, marked up for the pump's and motor's inefficiency. A real installation always draws more than the ideal fluid power.
example:
A pump lifts water at Q = 0.05 m³/s through h = 20 m with total efficiency eta_t = 0.70 (gamma = 9,790 N/m³).
Required power:
\(\dot{W} = \dfrac{Q\,\gamma\,h}{\eta_t}\)
\(\dot{W} = \dfrac{(0.05)(9{,}790)(20)}{0.70}\)
\(\dot{W} = \dfrac{9{,}790}{0.70} = 13{,}986\ \text{W} \approx 14.0\ \text{kW}\)

title: Specific weight and specific gravity of a fluid

symbols.gamma: specific weight: weight of fluid per unit volume
symbols.rho: density: mass of fluid per unit volume
symbols.SG: specific gravity: dimensionless ratio comparing the fluid to water

explanation: Specific weight is density with gravity folded in, and it is the version that appears in pressure equations. Specific gravity strips the units away entirely by comparing the fluid against water.
example:
An oil has density rho = 850 kg/m³.
Specific weight:
\(\gamma = \rho\,g\)
\(\gamma = (850)(9.81) = 8{,}339\ \text{N/m}^3 = 8.34\ \text{kN/m}^3\)
Specific gravity:
\(SG = \dfrac{\rho}{\rho_w} = \dfrac{850}{1000}\)
\(SG = 0.85\)

explanation: When every void in a soil sample holds water, the total unit weight rises to its saturated value, which blends the weight of the solids and the pore water through the void ratio.

symbols.G_s: specific gravity of the soil solids
symbols.γ_sat: saturated unit weight of the soil (all voids filled with water)

title: Saturated unit weight

example:
Field dry unit weight = 118 pcf, lab maximum = 124 pcf:
Step 1: RC = (118 / 124) × 100
Step 2: RC = 0.9516 × 100 = 95.2%
explanation: Relative compaction compares how dense the soil ended up in the field to the densest it became in the lab, so inspectors can check whether a fill meets the specification.

symbols.γ_D,field: dry unit weight measured in the field after compaction
symbols.γ_D,max: maximum dry unit weight from the laboratory compaction test

title: Relative compaction

explanation: As a clay layer squeezes pore water out under load, its voids shrink; the final settlement is that volumetric strain multiplied by the layer thickness.
section: Ultimate consolidation settlement in soil layer

symbols.H_S: thickness of the compressible soil layer
symbols.S_ULT: ultimate (long-term) consolidation settlement of the layer
symbols.Δe_TOT: total change in void ratio from recompression plus virgin compression
symbols.ε_v: vertical strain from the change in void ratio

explanation: Soil strength comes only from grain-to-grain contact, so the pore water pressure pushing the grains apart is subtracted from the total stress.

symbols.σ': effective stress, carried by the soil skeleton

title: Effective stress

explanation: A soil fails in shear when the shear stress on a plane reaches the soil's cohesive stickiness plus its frictional resistance, which grows with the normal stress.

symbols.σ_N: total normal stress acting on the failure plane
symbols.τ_f: shear stress on the plane at failure

title: Shear strength at failure (Mohr–Coulomb)

explanation: When a retaining wall yields outward, the soil behind it relaxes into the active state, and this coefficient scales the vertical stress down to the horizontal push.

symbols.K_A: Rankine active earth pressure coefficient (smooth wall, cohesionless soil, level backfill)

title: Rankine active earth pressure coefficient

explanation: The triangular active pressure distribution over a soil layer integrates to a single resultant force — the lateral load the wall must be designed to resist.

symbols.P_A1: active force per unit length of wall from the top soil layer
symbols.σ'_1: effective vertical stress at the base of layer 1

title: Active earth force on retaining wall

explanation: A footing fails when the soil beneath it shears along a rupture surface; the capacity adds up the cohesion term, the surcharge of soil above the base, and the weight of the failure wedge.

symbols.D_f: depth of footing below ground surface
symbols.N_γ: bearing capacity factor for unit weight
symbols.q_ULT: ultimate bearing capacity of the soil

explanation: A gravel earns the well-graded label when its particle sizes span a wide, smooth range instead of clustering at one size, which makes it pack into a denser, stronger fill.

example:

explanation: In moment distribution, half of an unbalanced moment applied at one end of a prismatic beam shows up at the fixed far end — the carryover factor is one-half.

explanation: The concrete compression zone is idealized as a uniform stress block whose depth is set so its total push exactly balances the tensile pull of the steel.

symbols.a: depth of the equivalent rectangular concrete stress block
symbols.b: width of the compression face of the member
symbols.f_y: yield strength of the steel reinforcement

explanation: Dividing the flow by the area gives the superficial velocity — the speed water would have if it moved through the full cross section, pores and grains alike.

explanation: Open-channel flow grows with area and slope but is held back by boundary roughness, with the hydraulic radius capturing how efficiently the channel shape conveys water.

symbols.K: unit constant, 1.486 for USCS units and 1.0 for SI units
